title: Asking with eikö ole with plural owners
summary: Ask negative possession questions with meillä, teillä, and heillä and fixed eikö … ole.
targetSkills: Fixed eikö ole in possession questions
objectives: Ask negative possession questions with meillä, teillä, and heillä and fixed eikö … ole.
Apply the pattern using the supporting forms shown.

sections.title: How the pattern works
paragraphs: Ask negative possession questions with meillä, teillä, and heillä and fixed eikö … ole.
Eikö is ei plus the question ending -kö. Put the owner between eikö and ole, then use the complete partitive noun: Eikö + owner + ole + thing.
keyPoints: Ask negative possession questions with meillä, teillä, and heillä and fixed eikö … ole.

steps: Several owners still use eikö … ole, not emmekö … ole.
meillä means “we as the owner”. Put this owner between eikö and ole.
Keep ole after the owner and the shown partitive autoa (“a car”) last.
The group owner teillä leaves eikö … ole unchanged, not ettekö … ole.
teillä means “you as the owner” for a group. Put this owner between eikö and ole.
Keep ole after the owner and the shown partitive peliä (“a game”) last.
Heillä leaves eikö … ole unchanged, not eivätkö … ole.
heillä means “they as the owner”. Put this owner between eikö and ole.
Keep ole after the owner and the shown partitive kynää (“a pen”) last.
The noun and ei each follow their own vowel rule; the noun does not choose the -kö in eikö.
meillä means “we as the owner”. Put this owner between eikö and ole.
Keep ole after the owner and the shown partitive tyynyä (“a pillow”) last.
teillä identifies the plural owner in this asking with eikö ole with plural owners pattern.
Use Eikö + owner + ole; the negative question keeps this fixed verb pattern.
kirjaa (“a book”) is the complete regular singular partitive: kirja + -a.
teillä identifies the plural owner in this asking with eikö ole with plural owners pattern.
Use Eikö + owner + ole; the negative question keeps this fixed verb pattern.
kissaa (“a cat”) is the complete regular singular partitive: kissa + -a.
heillä identifies the plural owner in this asking with eikö ole with plural owners pattern.
Use Eikö + owner + ole; the negative question keeps this fixed verb pattern.
koiraa (“a dog”) is the complete regular singular partitive: koira + -a.

commonMistakes: Use fixed eikö with every owner, including groups; do not replace it with emmekö or eivätkö.
Keep the shown partitive noun after the negative question pattern: palloa, rather than pallo.

practiceExercises.prompt: Optional practice: Translate “Eikö heillä ole palloa?” into English. Owner: they.
acceptedAnswers: Do they not have a ball?
Do they not have the ball?
practiceExercises.explanation: The -lla/-llä phrase identifies the owner; eikö … ole stays fixed in this possession pattern.

sentenceExplanation.pattern: eikö + possessor + fixed ole + singular partitive noun

parts.formation: Ei + the question ending -kö = eikö. The front-vowel ending follows ei, independently of the noun.

parts.role: possessor: the person who has the thing
parts.formation: he has the learned possession form heillä; its -lla/-llä ending marks the possessor. Learn this pronoun form as a whole.
Negative possession keeps ole after eikö, with every owner.
pallo + -a = palloa. This is the singular partitive, the noun form used when possession is denied.

practiceExercises.prompt: Optional practice: Translate “Eikö meillä ole autoa?” into English. Owner: we.
acceptedAnswers: Do we not have a car?
Do we not have the car?
